slides.heading: The Science Behind Intermittent Fasting
slides.body: What happens inside your body when you skip meals — and why millions swear by it

slides.heading: What Is Intermittent Fasting?
slides.body: Intermittent fasting (IF) is an eating pattern that cycles between periods of fasting and eating. It doesn't prescribe which foods to eat, but rather when you eat them. Popular schedules include 16:8 (16 hours fast, 8 hours eating window) and 5:2 (normal eating 5 days, restricted calories 2 days).

slides.heading: The Metabolic Switch
slides.body: After 12–16 hours without food, your body depletes liver glycogen and switches to burning fat for fuel. This state — called ketosis — produces ketone bodies that efficiently power your brain and muscles. The metabolic switch is at the core of IF's benefits.

slides.heading: Autophagy: The Body's Self-Cleaning Mode
slides.body: Fasting triggers autophagy, a cellular recycling process where the body breaks down and removes damaged proteins and organelles. This natural 'clean-up' is linked to reduced inflammation, slower aging, and lower cancer risk. Nobel Prize winner Yoshinori Ohsumi's research illuminated this mechanism in 2016.

slides.heading: Hormonal Changes During Fasting
slides.body: Fasting dramatically lowers insulin levels, making stored fat more accessible. At the same time, human growth hormone (HGH) can surge up to 5-fold, supporting muscle preservation and fat metabolism. Norepinephrine also rises, boosting metabolic rate to keep you energized while fasting.

slides.heading: Benefits Backed by Research
slides.body: Studies consistently link IF to weight loss, reduced belly fat, lower LDL cholesterol, and improved insulin sensitivity. Research in animals shows significant lifespan extension. In humans, trials demonstrate reductions in blood pressure and markers of chronic inflammation within weeks of starting.

slides.heading: Impact on the Brain
slides.body: Fasting boosts production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein that supports neuron growth and protects against cognitive decline. Animal studies show IF may reduce the risk of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Many practitioners also report sharper focus and mental clarity during fasted states.

slides.heading: Who Should Be Cautious
slides.body: IF is not for everyone. Pregnant or breastfeeding women, people with a history of eating disorders, type 1 diabetics, and those underweight should avoid it or consult a doctor first. Some people experience headaches, irritability, or fatigue initially — most side effects subside after the first week of adjustment.

slides.heading: Tips for Getting Started
slides.body: Begin with a 12-hour overnight fast and gradually extend to 14–16 hours. Stay well-hydrated with water, black coffee, or plain tea. Break your fast with whole foods — proteins, healthy fats, and vegetables. Consistency matters more than perfection; most benefits appear after 4–8 weeks of regular practice.

slides.heading: Fast Smart, Live Better
slides.body: Intermittent fasting isn't a trend — it's a biologically grounded eating strategy. Whether your goal is weight loss, mental clarity, or longevity, the science suggests that giving your body a break from food may be one of the simplest health upgrades available.
